prompt: Which type of blood vessel carries blood **away** from the heart?
hints: The three types of blood vessel are arteries, veins and capillaries.
solution: **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry blood back to the heart.

prompt: What is the name for the tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens?
hints: They are at the very ends of the smallest airways (the bronchioles).
solution: The **alveoli** (one is an alveolus). Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way.

prompt: Put these parts of the digestive system in the order that food passes through them.
hints: The oesophagus is the tube from your mouth to your stomach.
The small intestine comes before the large intestine.
solution: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

prompt: Which part of the blood carries most of the oxygen around the body?

options.text: Red blood cells
White blood cells
Platelets
Plasma

feedback.b: White blood cells help fight infection.
feedback.d: Plasma carries dissolved substances such as glucose and carbon dioxide, but very little oxygen.

hints: Oxygen is carried by a red substance called haemoglobin.
solution: **Red blood cells** contain haemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the body's tissues.

prompt: Match each part of the blood to its job.

right.text: Carries dissolved food, carbon dioxide and wastes

hints: Plasma is the yellowish liquid part of the blood.
solution: Red blood cells → carry oxygen. White blood cells → fight infection. Platelets → clotting. Plasma → carries dissolved substances such as glucose, carbon dioxide and urea.

prompt: The enzyme [[a]] breaks down starch into sugars. Protease enzymes break down proteins into [[b]].
hints: Lipase works on fats.
Proteins are long chains of smaller building blocks.
solution: **Amylase** breaks starch into sugars. Protease breaks proteins into **amino acids**. Lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

prompt: What is the name of the sheet of muscle under the lungs that helps you breathe?
hints: It separates the chest from the abdomen.
solution: The **diaphragm**. When it contracts, it flattens, which makes the chest bigger and draws air into the lungs.

prompt: In which organ are most digested food molecules absorbed into the blood?

options.text: Small intestine
Stomach
Large intestine
Oesophagus

feedback.b: The stomach churns food and starts digesting protein, but very little food is absorbed there.
feedback.c: The large intestine mainly absorbs water.
feedback.d: The oesophagus just moves food down to the stomach.

hints: This organ is lined with millions of tiny finger-like villi.
solution: Digested food is absorbed in the **small intestine**. Its lining has millions of villi, which give it a huge surface area, thin walls and a rich blood supply.

prompt: Select **all** the features of alveoli that make gas exchange fast and efficient.

options.text: Very thin walls (one cell thick)
A very large total surface area
A moist lining
A rich supply of blood capillaries
Thick, muscular walls
Rings of cartilage to keep them open

hints: Gases move in and out of the alveoli by diffusion. What makes diffusion faster?
Cartilage rings are found in the trachea, not the alveoli.
solution: Alveoli have **thin walls** (short distance), a **huge surface area**, a **moist lining** (gases dissolve before diffusing) and a **rich blood supply** (keeps the concentration difference high). Thick walls would slow diffusion down. Cartilage rings hold open the trachea, not the alveoli.

prompt: Why does the left ventricle of the heart have a thicker, more muscular wall than the right ventricle?

options.text: It pumps blood all the way around the body, which needs more pressure
It pumps blood only to the lungs, which are close to the heart
It holds a lot more blood than the right ventricle does
It receives blood straight from the body through the veins

feedback.b: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. That trip is short, so it needs less force.
feedback.c: Both ventricles pump about the same volume of blood with each beat. The left one pumps it harder.
feedback.d: Blood from the body returns to the right atrium, not the left ventricle.

hints: Where does each ventricle send its blood?
Which journey is longer?
solution: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood to the **whole body**, so it needs to create a much higher pressure. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

prompt: Capillary walls are only [[a]] cell thick, so substances such as oxygen and glucose can [[b]] quickly between the blood and the body's cells.
hints: The thinner the wall, the shorter the distance substances have to travel.
solution: Capillary walls are only **one** cell thick, so oxygen and glucose can **diffuse** quickly out of the blood into the cells. Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way.

prompt: When you breathe in, the diaphragm [[a]] and flattens, and the ribs move up and out. The volume inside the chest [[b]], so air flows into the lungs.
hints: Muscles do work by contracting.
Air flows in when there is more space inside the chest, because the pressure inside drops.
solution: Breathing in: the diaphragm **contracts** and flattens, and the rib muscles pull the ribs up and out. The chest volume **increases**, the pressure inside drops, and air flows in.

prompt: How is the air you breathe out different from the air you breathe in?

options.text: It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
It has no oxygen left in it at all
It has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide
Its gases are exactly the same; it is just warmer

feedback.b: Breathed-out air still has about 16% oxygen. That's why rescue breathing can help someone.
feedback.c: This is the wrong way round. Your body takes oxygen in and gives carbon dioxide out.
feedback.d: Breathed-out air is warmer, but the amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide change too.

hints: Your cells use one gas for respiration and make the other as waste.
solution:
| Gas | Breathed in | Breathed out |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | about 21% | about 16% |
| Carbon dioxide | about 0.04% | about 4% |

Breathed-out air has **less oxygen** and **more carbon dioxide**. It is also warmer and contains more water vapour.

prompt: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces without changing the chemicals in it. What type of digestion is this?
hints: The other type, chemical digestion, uses enzymes.
solution: This is **mechanical** (physical) digestion. Smaller pieces have a bigger surface area, so enzymes can then digest the food faster (chemical digestion).

prompt: Sione counts 21 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is his heart rate in beats per minute?
hints: How many lots of 15 seconds are in one minute?
solution: There are 4 lots of 15 seconds in a minute, so $21 \times 4 = 84$ beats per minute.

prompt: Veins contain valves. What do the valves do?

options.text: Stop blood from flowing backwards
Pump blood back to the heart
Add oxygen to the blood
Raise the blood pressure in the veins

feedback.b: The heart is the pump. Valves are flaps that only let blood go one way.
feedback.c: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs.
feedback.d: Blood pressure in veins is low. That's exactly why the valves are needed.

hints: Blood in veins is at low pressure, and much of it has to travel upwards to the heart.
solution: Blood in veins is at **low pressure**, so it could flow backwards. Valves are flaps that only open one way, which keeps the blood moving towards the heart.

prompt: A muscle cell needs glucose and oxygen for respiration. Explain how the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems work together to supply it.
modelAnswer: Respiration in the muscle cell needs glucose and oxygen: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). The digestive system breaks down food, such as starch, into small glucose molecules, which are absorbed into the blood through the wall of the small intestine. The respiratory system brings air into the alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into the blood in the capillaries, and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be breathed out. The circulatory system carries the glucose and oxygen in the blood, pumped by the heart, to the muscle. In the capillaries, they diffuse into the muscle cell, and the carbon dioxide it makes is carried away.

rubric.criterion: States that respiration needs glucose and oxygen (or gives the word equation)
Describes the digestive system breaking food into glucose that is absorbed into the blood in the small intestine
Describes the respiratory system: oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood (and carbon dioxide is removed)
Describes the circulatory system: the heart pumps blood carrying glucose and oxygen to the muscle, where they pass into the cell through the capillaries

hints: Start with the word equation for respiration.
For each system, say what it supplies and how that substance gets into the blood.
solution: Digestive system → glucose into the blood. Respiratory system → oxygen into the blood (and carbon dioxide out). Circulatory system → heart and blood vessels deliver both to the muscle cell, through the capillaries.

prompt: During a netball game, Losa's heart rate and breathing rate both increase. Explain why.
modelAnswer: Losa's muscles are working harder, so they need to release more energy by respiration. Respiration needs glucose and oxygen, so these must be delivered to the muscles faster. The muscles also make more carbon dioxide, which must be removed. A faster heart rate pumps blood around the body more quickly, delivering more oxygen and glucose to the muscles and carrying carbon dioxide away. Faster, deeper breathing brings more oxygen into the lungs and gets rid of more carbon dioxide.

rubric.criterion: States that the muscles respire more to release more energy
States that more oxygen (and glucose) must be delivered and more carbon dioxide removed
Links the faster heart rate to faster blood flow, and the faster breathing to more gas exchange in the lungs

hints: What do working muscles need more of?
What does the heart do, and what do the lungs do, to help?
solution: More exercise → more respiration in muscles → more oxygen and glucose needed, more carbon dioxide made. The heart beats faster to deliver blood faster, and breathing speeds up to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

prompt: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs. What is unusual about this artery?

options.text: It carries blood that is low in oxygen
It carries blood towards the heart
It has valves all along its length, like a vein
Its walls are only one cell thick

feedback.b: All arteries, including this one, carry blood away from the heart.
feedback.c: Valves all along a vessel are a feature of veins. Arteries don't need them, because their blood is at high pressure.
feedback.d: Walls one cell thick are a feature of capillaries.

hints: Why is blood going to the lungs?
solution: Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood to the body. The pulmonary artery carries **oxygen-poor blood** from the right ventricle to the lungs, to pick up oxygen. It is still an artery, because it carries blood **away** from the heart.

prompt: Hana tests how fast a human digestive enzyme works at 20 °C, 37 °C and 60 °C. What result is most likely?

options.text: Fastest at 37 °C, and very slow or stopped at 60 °C
Fastest at 60 °C, because heat always speeds up reactions
The same at all three, because enzymes are not used up
Fastest at 20 °C, because enzymes work best when cool

feedback.b: Heat only speeds up enzyme reactions up to a point. At high temperatures the enzyme's shape is damaged (it is denatured) and it stops working.
feedback.c: Enzymes aren't used up, but how fast they work still depends on temperature.
feedback.d: Cooler temperatures slow enzymes down. Human enzymes work best at body temperature.

hints: What is the normal temperature inside the human body?
solution: Human enzymes work best at about **37 °C**, body temperature. At 20 °C they work more slowly. At 60 °C the enzyme's shape is damaged (**denatured**), so it stops working.

prompt: In the lung disease emphysema, which is often caused by smoking, the walls between alveoli break down. The lungs end up with fewer, larger air sacs. Why does this make a person breathless?

options.text: The total surface area for gas exchange is smaller, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood
The larger air sacs hold more air, so too much oxygen enters the blood
The heart has to pump air into the lungs instead of pumping blood
The diaphragm stops working once the alveoli have broken down

feedback.b: The problem is surface area, not the volume of air. Less surface area means less oxygen gets into the blood.
feedback.c: The heart pumps blood, never air. Air is moved by breathing.
feedback.d: The diaphragm still works. The problem is in the alveoli, where gas exchange happens.

hints: Think about why it is useful to have millions of tiny alveoli rather than a few big ones.
What happens to the rate of diffusion if the surface area gets smaller?
solution: Millions of tiny alveoli give a huge surface area. Fewer, larger sacs have a much **smaller total surface area**, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood with each breath. The person's cells don't get enough oxygen, so they feel breathless.

prompt: Sofia fills a bag of Visking tubing with starch solution and the enzyme amylase. She puts the bag into a beaker of warm water. After 30 minutes, she tests the water outside the bag: it contains sugar, but no starch. What does this show?

options.text: Amylase broke the starch into sugar, which is small enough to pass through the tubing, like the wall of the small intestine
Starch passed through the tubing first, and then it turned into sugar in the water outside
The warm water broke down the starch by itself, so the enzyme wasn't needed at all
The sugar was already in the water at the start, because sugar can't pass through the tubing

feedback.b: There was no starch in the water, so the starch didn't pass through the tubing.
feedback.c: Starch breaks down extremely slowly in water alone. The amylase did the work. (A control bag with no amylase would show this.)
feedback.d: The sugar came from digesting the starch, and it is small enough to pass through the tubing.

hints: Starch molecules are very large. Sugar molecules are small.
What does amylase do to starch?
solution: Starch molecules are too big to pass through the tiny holes in the tubing. **Amylase** digested the starch into small sugar molecules, which passed through into the water. This is a model of the gut: food must be digested into small, soluble molecules before it can be absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.

prompt: Put these in order to show the path of an oxygen molecule from the air to a muscle cell in your leg.

items.text: Red blood cell in a lung capillary

hints: The airways branch into smaller and smaller tubes.
Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs.
solution: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchus → bronchiole → alveolus → (diffuses into) red blood cell in a lung capillary → (carried by the circulatory system to) muscle cell.

prompt: Which gas passes from the alveoli into the blood?

options.text: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Water vapour

feedback.b: Carbon dioxide moves the other way: from the blood into the alveoli, so it can be breathed out.
feedback.c: Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but the body doesn't use it, so there is no overall movement of nitrogen into the blood.
feedback.d: Water vapour is mostly breathed **out**, not taken in.

hints: Which gas do your cells need for respiration?
solution: **Oxygen** diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, where there is less of it. Carbon dioxide diffuses the opposite way, from the blood into the alveoli.

prompt: What is the name of the tube that carries air from your mouth and nose down towards your lungs?
hints: It has rings of cartilage to keep it open, and you can feel them at the front of your neck.
solution: The **trachea** (windpipe) carries air down to the lungs, where it divides into two bronchi.

prompt: What is the name of the muscular tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach?
hints: It runs down your neck and chest, just behind the windpipe.
solution: The **oesophagus** (gullet) carries food to the stomach. Its muscles squeeze the food along in waves.

prompt: [[a]] carry blood away from the heart. [[b]] carry blood back to the heart. Substances pass between the blood and the body's cells through the thin walls of [[c]].
hints: Which vessels have walls only one cell thick?
Of the other two, which one has valves to stop blood flowing backwards on its way back to the heart?
solution: **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart. **Veins** return it to the heart. **Capillaries** have walls only one cell thick, so substances such as oxygen and glucose can pass through them to the cells.

prompt: Select **all** the substances that are carried mainly in the **plasma** (the liquid part of the blood).

options.text: Glucose
Carbon dioxide
Urea (a waste made in the liver)
Hormones, such as insulin
Oxygen
Starch

hints: Plasma carries things that are dissolved in it.
Which substance is carried mostly by red blood cells?
solution:
Plasma carries dissolved substances: digested food such as **glucose**, **carbon dioxide**, wastes such as **urea**, and **hormones**.

Most **oxygen** is carried by the red blood cells, not the plasma. **Starch** molecules are too big to be absorbed into the blood: starch is digested into glucose first.

stem:
Ana investigates how exercise affects her pulse rate. She counts her pulse for 15 seconds at rest, then does star jumps for 2 minutes. She counts her pulse for 15 seconds straight after stopping, and again every minute after that.

| Time | Beats counted in 15 s |
|---|---|
| At rest, before exercise | 18 |
| Straight after exercise | 35 |
| 1 minute after stopping | 29 |
| 2 minutes after stopping | 24 |
| 3 minutes after stopping | 20 |
| 4 minutes after stopping | 18 |
prompt: What is the **dependent** variable in Ana's investigation?

options.text: Her pulse rate
The time since she stopped exercising
The type of exercise (star jumps)
How long she exercised for (2 minutes)

feedback.b: This is the **independent** variable: Ana chooses the times when she takes each count.
feedback.c: This stays the same throughout, so it is a controlled variable.
feedback.d: This stays the same throughout, so it is a controlled variable.

hints: The dependent variable is the one you measure to get your results.
solution: The **dependent variable** is what Ana measures: her **pulse rate**. The independent variable is the time since she stopped exercising. The type and length of exercise are controlled variables.

prompt: What was Ana's resting heart rate, in beats per minute?
hints: She counted for 15 seconds. How many lots of 15 seconds are there in one minute?
solution: 60 s ÷ 15 s = 4, so multiply the count by 4: $18 \times 4 = 72$ beats per minute.

prompt: By how many beats per minute did Ana's heart rate increase, from rest to straight after exercise?
hints: Convert both counts to beats per minute first (multiply by 4).
Then find the difference.
solution:
Straight after exercise: $35 \times 4 = 140$ bpm. At rest: $18 \times 4 = 72$ bpm.

Increase $= 140 - 72 = 68$ beats per minute.

prompt: Suggest **two** ways Ana could improve her investigation. For at least one of them, explain how it would make her results more reliable or accurate.
modelAnswer:
1. Repeat the whole investigation several times (for example, on different days) and calculate the mean for each time. Then one unusual result or counting mistake has much less effect, so the results are more reliable.

2. Use a heart-rate monitor instead of counting by hand. When a 15-second count is multiplied by 4, any counting mistake is multiplied by 4 too.

(Other good improvements: do the star jumps at the same steady speed every time, or make sure she has rested fully before she starts.)

rubric.criterion: Gives one valid improvement (e.g. repeat and find the mean; use a heart-rate monitor; keep the exercise at the same speed; rest fully first)
Gives a second, different valid improvement
Explains how an improvement helps (e.g. averaging reduces the effect of a one-off error; multiplying a 15 s count by 4 multiplies any mistake by 4)

hints: Is one set of results from one person enough to be sure?
Counting a pulse by hand for 15 seconds can easily be out by one beat. What happens to that error when you multiply by 4?
solution: Good improvements include **repeating and averaging**, **measuring more accurately** (for example, with a heart-rate monitor) and **controlling variables** such as the speed of the star jumps. Always explain **why** each one helps.

prompt: Arteries have thick, muscular, stretchy walls. Why?

options.text: Blood in arteries is under high pressure from the heart's pumping
Thick walls let oxygen pass out of the arteries more quickly
Arteries carry blood back to the heart from far parts of the body
Thick walls stop the blood in arteries from flowing backwards

feedback.b: Substances pass in and out of the blood through **capillaries**, whose walls are very thin. Thick walls would slow this down.
feedback.c: Arteries carry blood **away** from the heart. Veins bring it back.
feedback.d: Backflow is stopped by valves. Veins have valves along their length; arteries rely on high pressure instead.

hints: Think about what happens inside an artery every time the heart beats.
solution: Each heartbeat pushes blood into the arteries at **high pressure**. Thick, muscular, elastic walls can withstand this pressure, stretching and springing back with each beat. That stretch is what you feel as your pulse.

prompt: Why does the stomach make hydrochloric acid?

options.text: It kills most bacteria in food and gives the right conditions for stomach enzymes
It breaks down the starch in food into glucose, ready for absorption
It neutralises the food, so that the food doesn't damage the stomach
It absorbs digested food through the stomach wall into the blood

feedback.b: Starch is broken down by the enzyme amylase, in the mouth and small intestine, not by acid.
feedback.c: Acid makes the stomach contents **more** acidic, not neutral. A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall.
feedback.d: Digested food is absorbed mainly in the small intestine.

hints: Think about what might be living on your food, and about the enzyme that works in the stomach.
solution: Hydrochloric acid **kills most of the bacteria** swallowed with food, and it gives the **acidic conditions** that the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme needs to work well.

prompt: Many people mix up **breathing** and **respiration**. Explain the difference between them.
modelAnswer: Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, caused by the diaphragm and rib muscles. It is a physical process. Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens inside every living cell, in which glucose reacts with oxygen to release energy (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water). Breathing supplies the oxygen that respiration needs and removes the carbon dioxide it makes.

rubric.criterion: Describes breathing as moving air into and out of the lungs
Describes respiration as a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose (using oxygen)

hints: Where does each one happen: in the lungs, or in every cell?
Which one releases energy?
solution: **Breathing** = moving air in and out of the lungs. **Respiration** = the chemical reaction in every cell that releases energy from glucose. Breathing supports respiration by bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide.

prompt: Which enzyme breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol?

options.text: Lipase
Amylase
Protease
Bile

feedback.b: Amylase breaks down starch into sugars.
feedback.c: Protease breaks down proteins into amino acids.
feedback.d: Bile breaks fat into small droplets, which helps lipase to work, but bile is not an enzyme.

hints: Fats and oils are also called lipids.
solution: **Lipase** breaks down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile helps by breaking fat into tiny droplets, giving lipase a bigger surface to work on.

stem:
Kahu investigates how temperature affects amylase, the enzyme that breaks down starch. She mixes starch solution and amylase in test tubes kept at different temperatures. Every 30 seconds, she puts a drop of each mixture onto iodine solution. When the iodine no longer turns blue-black, all of the starch has been broken down.

| Temperature (°C) | Time for the starch to disappear (minutes) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 12 |
| 20 | 7 |
| 30 | 4 |
| 40 | 2 |
| 50 | 6 |
| 60 | Starch still there after 20 minutes |
prompt: At which temperature did the amylase break down the starch fastest? Give your answer in °C.
hints: The fastest reaction takes the **shortest** time.
solution: The shortest time (2 minutes) was at **40 °C**, so the amylase worked fastest at this temperature.

prompt: Why didn't the amylase break down the starch at 60 °C?

options.text: The high temperature changed the enzyme's shape, so it no longer worked
The high temperature killed the enzyme, because enzymes are living things
The particles had so much energy that they moved too fast to react
The starch evaporated before the enzyme had time to break it down

feedback.b: Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they can't be killed. High temperatures change their shape permanently instead (they are denatured).
feedback.c: Heating particles normally speeds reactions up. The problem is that the enzyme's shape has been changed.
feedback.d: Starch doesn't evaporate at 60 °C. The iodine test showed that the starch was still there.

hints: Enzymes are proteins with a very particular shape.
solution: An enzyme has a particular shape that fits the molecules it works on. At 60 °C, the amylase's shape is changed permanently: it is **denatured**, so it can no longer break down the starch.

prompt: Hemi says, "This proves that the best temperature for amylase is exactly 40 °C." Explain why the results don't show this, and how Kahu could find the best temperature more precisely.
modelAnswer: Kahu only tested every 10 °C, so the best (optimum) temperature could be anywhere between about 30 °C and 50 °C: for example, it could be 37 °C. To find it more precisely, she should test more temperatures in that range, such as every 2 °C from 30 °C to 50 °C, and repeat each test to check her results.

rubric.criterion: Explains why the results do not prove exactly 40 °C (e.g. temperatures were only tested every 10 °C, so the best temperature could be anywhere between about 30 °C and 50 °C; each temperature was only tested once)
Suggests testing smaller steps of temperature between 30 °C and 50 °C (and repeating the tests)

hints: Which temperatures did Kahu actually test?
Could the best temperature be one that she never tested?
solution: The results only show that the optimum is **somewhere between 30 °C and 50 °C**. Testing **smaller temperature steps** in that range (and repeating) would pin it down. (Human amylase actually works best at about body temperature, 37 °C.)

prompt: Put these in order to show the path of blood through the heart and lungs, starting with blood that has just come back from the body.
hints: Blood from the body enters the right side of the heart.
In each side, blood goes into an atrium (upper chamber) before a ventricle (lower chamber).
solution: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (blood picks up oxygen) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → out to the body.

prompt: Cigarette smoke contains carbon monoxide, which attaches to red blood cells in place of oxygen. Why do smokers often get out of breath more quickly when they exercise?

options.text: Their blood carries less oxygen to their muscles for respiration
Carbon monoxide blocks the trachea, so less air can get in
Their lungs take in too much oxygen, which damages the lungs
Carbon monoxide makes the heart beat much more slowly

feedback.b: Carbon monoxide is a gas. It doesn't block the airways; it affects the red blood cells.
feedback.c: The problem is that **less** oxygen is carried, not too much.
feedback.d: With less oxygen in the blood, the heart tends to beat **faster**, to try to deliver enough oxygen.

hints: What is the job of red blood cells?
solution: Red blood cells carrying carbon monoxide can't carry as much oxygen. The muscles get less oxygen for respiration, so they can't release energy as well, and the smoker becomes breathless sooner as the body tries to take in more oxygen.

prompt: Carbon dioxide is made in a muscle cell in your leg. Explain how the circulatory system and the respiratory system work together to get rid of it.
modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide is made by respiration in the muscle cell. There is more carbon dioxide in the cell than in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood in a nearby capillary. The blood (mostly the plasma) carries it through the veins back to the heart, which pumps it to the lungs. In the lungs, there is less carbon dioxide in the air in the alveoli than in the blood, so it diffuses out of the capillaries into the alveoli, and it is breathed out.

rubric.criterion: States that carbon dioxide is made by respiration and diffuses from the muscle cell into the blood in a capillary
Describes the blood (plasma) carrying it in veins to the heart, which pumps it to the lungs
Describes carbon dioxide diffusing from the blood into the alveoli, and being breathed out

hints: Start in the muscle cell: which process makes carbon dioxide, and how does it get into the blood?
Finish in the lungs: how does it leave the blood?
solution: Muscle cell (respiration) → **diffuses** into a capillary → carried in the plasma through **veins** → **heart** pumps it to the lungs → **diffuses** into the alveoli → **breathed out**.

prompt: In which labelled organ does the digestion of **protein** begin?

options.text: Organ B
Organ A
Organ D
Organ E

feedback.a: The oesophagus just moves food down to the stomach by squeezing it along. No protein is digested there.
feedback.d: Protein digestion continues in the small intestine, but it **begins** before the food gets there.
feedback.e: By the time food reaches the large intestine, digestion is almost finished. Here, water is absorbed from what is left.

hints: Protein digestion needs a protease enzyme and acidic conditions.
solution: Protein digestion begins in the **stomach (B)**. The stomach makes a protease enzyme and hydrochloric acid, which gives the acidic conditions that the enzyme needs.

prompt: The inside wall of the small intestine (D) is covered in millions of tiny, finger-like **villi**. Explain how villi help to absorb digested food into the blood.
modelAnswer: Villi greatly increase the surface area of the small intestine wall, so much more digested food (such as glucose and amino acids) can be absorbed at the same time. The wall of each villus is very thin, only one cell thick, so food molecules have only a short distance to travel into the blood. Each villus also has a network of blood capillaries, so the blood quickly carries the absorbed food away. This keeps the concentration in the blood low, so absorption keeps going.

rubric.criterion: States that villi give a large surface area for absorption
States that the villus walls are thin (one cell thick), so food molecules have a short distance to travel
Explains that a good blood supply (capillaries) carries the absorbed food away, keeping a concentration difference so absorption continues

hints: Think about surface area, distance and blood supply.
Compare villi with the alveoli in the lungs.
solution: Villi are adapted like alveoli: **large surface area**, **thin walls** (short distance) and a **rich blood supply** that carries absorbed food away.

prompt: At high altitude, each breath contains less oxygen than at sea level. After a few weeks living high in the mountains, a climber's body makes extra red blood cells. How does this help the climber?

options.text: More red blood cells can carry more oxygen from each breath to the muscles
More red blood cells can make extra oxygen for the body to use
More red blood cells carry away more carbon dioxide, so the climber breathes less
More red blood cells mean the heart doesn't need to pump as often

feedback.b: Red blood cells carry oxygen; they don't make it. The only source of oxygen is the air the climber breathes in.
feedback.c: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the plasma, and the problem at altitude is getting enough oxygen, not removing carbon dioxide.
feedback.d: The heart still has to pump the blood around the body. Extra red blood cells help each beat deliver more oxygen.

hints: What is the job of red blood cells?
What does the climber need more of at altitude?
solution: Red blood cells carry **oxygen** from the lungs to the cells. With more red blood cells, the blood can pick up and carry more of the oxygen that is available, so the muscles get enough oxygen for respiration.

prompt: The heart muscle gets its blood from the coronary arteries. In a heart attack, one of these arteries becomes blocked. Explain why part of the heart muscle can stop working, or die.
modelAnswer: The coronary arteries carry blood with oxygen and glucose to the heart muscle cells. If an artery is blocked, the muscle cells beyond the blockage don't get oxygen and glucose, so they can't carry out respiration to release energy. Without energy, the muscle cells can't contract, and if the blockage lasts too long they die. That part of the heart can no longer help to pump blood.

rubric.criterion: States that the coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood carrying oxygen and glucose
Explains that without oxygen and glucose, the muscle cells can't respire to release energy
Explains that without energy, the cells can't contract (and die), so the heart can't pump properly

hints: The heart muscle works all the time. What do its cells need to keep releasing energy?
What happens to the cells if that supply stops?
solution: Blocked coronary artery → no **oxygen** or **glucose** for that part of the heart muscle → no **respiration**, so no energy → the muscle can't **contract** and may die.

prompt: At rest, Liam takes 12 breaths per minute, and each breath moves 0.5 L of air into his lungs. During hard exercise, he takes 30 breaths per minute, and each breath moves 2.5 L of air. How many times as much air does he breathe in each minute during exercise as at rest?
hints: Air per minute = number of breaths per minute × volume of each breath.
Work this out at rest and during exercise, then divide.
solution:
At rest: $12 \times 0.5 = 6$ L per minute.

During exercise: $30 \times 2.5 = 75$ L per minute.

$75 \div 6 = 12.5$, so he breathes **12.5 times** as much air each minute.
